subject: system-design
title: Design a Code Deployment System
summary: Build code into artifacts and roll them out to a global fleet of thousands of hosts safely. The hard parts are distributing big artifacts fast and limiting the blast radius of a bad release.

blocks.text: A code deployment system takes a commit, builds it into a deployable artifact, and pushes that artifact onto thousands of servers around the world without taking the service down. Two things make it hard: getting large artifacts to many hosts quickly, and rolling out changes so that a bad build hits a few hosts instead of all of them. Safety and speed of distribution are the whole game.

items: Build a commit into a versioned, immutable artifact and store it.
Distribute that artifact to a global fleet of hosts efficiently.
Deploy with minimal risk, so a bad release affects as few hosts as possible.
Roll back fast, and manage configuration alongside the code.

blocks.text: Picture tens of thousands of hosts across many regions and hundreds of deploys a day. Artifacts can be hundreds of megabytes to several gigabytes, so naively pulling from one origin would saturate it and make rollouts crawl. The dominant cost is moving a lot of bytes to a lot of hosts, fast, without a thundering herd hammering a single source.

A pipeline runs build → store → distribute → deploy. A build service compiles and tests the commit and produces an immutable, versioned artifact. That artifact lands in an artifact store (blob storage), then fans out through regional caches and a CDN so hosts pull from something nearby. A lightweight deploy agent on each host fetches its assigned version, swaps it in behind a health check, and reports status to a controller that drives the rollout.

items: Build service: compile and test a commit; emit an immutable, versioned artifact.
Artifact store: durable blob storage as the single source of truth for every version.
Distribution: regional caches and a CDN (or peer-to-peer) so hosts pull bytes locally, not from one origin.
Deploy agent: per-host process that pulls its target version, swaps it, health-checks, and reports back.
Deploy controller: orchestrates the rollout strategy and triggers rollback on failing health signals.

blocks.text: You never flip the whole fleet at once. Instead you advance the new version through the hosts in a controlled order, watching health and error metrics at each step, and stop or reverse the moment something looks wrong:

items: Rolling: update hosts in batches, draining and replacing a slice at a time so capacity stays up.
Blue-green: stand up the new version on a parallel fleet, then switch traffic over for instant cutover and instant rollback.
Canary: release to a tiny slice first, watch real metrics, and only widen if it stays healthy.
Health checks gate every step, and a regression triggers automatic rollback to the last known-good version.

blocks.title: Canary first
blocks.text: A canary deploy sends the new version to a small slice of hosts or users and watches error rates, latency, and key business metrics before going wider. If the canary regresses, you roll back having affected a fraction of traffic instead of everyone. It is the cheapest insurance against a bad build reaching the whole fleet.

Pushing a multi-gigabyte artifact to tens of thousands of hosts from one origin is the bottleneck, so you spread the load: cache the artifact in each region, serve it through a CDN, or let hosts share pieces peer-to-peer so the origin is read a handful of times rather than thousands. Configuration is versioned and shipped on the same disciplined path as code, because a bad config can break a fleet just as fast as a bad binary.

blocks.title: Takeaway
blocks.text: A deployment system is a build-and-distribute pipeline wrapped in safety. Produce immutable versioned artifacts, fan them out through regional caches and CDNs so distribution scales, and roll out via canary or blue-green with health checks and automatic rollback so a bad release is contained, not catastrophic.
